newsitem.title: USA: US base metals steady, quiet as seasonal lull nears.
newsitem.headline: US base metals steady, quiet as seasonal lull nears.

text.p: Physical trading on the U.S. base metals markets lacked major feature during the past Thanksgiving holiday week, though premiums remained steady.
Premiums on zinc continued at 5.25 to 6.00 cents per pound over LME cash.
"Although the LME price stinks, premiums have held up over five cents for an extended period which reflects that business is still good," a trader said. "Forward sales for 1997 are also strong."
Aluminum premiums remain at 4.00 to 4.25 cents per pound over LME cash, with a sizeable sale concluded this week for first quarter delivery at 4.25 cents, traders said.
But one dealer suggested the bottom end of the premium range was nearer 3.75 cents.
Benchmark A380 alloy prices have continued to firm a touch as secondary smelters struggle to improve their margins in the wake of higher aluminum scrap prices.
A Midwest smelter official said no business would be concluded under 70 cents per pound. "We don't really see the market come off. December is pretty well booked up," the official said.
Tin was ticking over but one trader said it was disappointing that LME three-months was unable to stay at $6,100 per tonne.

"It did not last very long, which was disillusioning for the customers who see no reason to jump and buy," a merchant said. Other traders noted the arrival of the first small batch of Grade A tin from Minsur's new smelter in Peru, still going through its start-up phase.
Tin premiums were quoted at 6 to 8 cents per pound over LME on Grade A metal, and 8 to 10 cents on low lead.
Nickel premiums remain at 8 to 12 cents per pound over LME cash, as the stainless scrap price for December moved sideways from November levels of $735 to $740 per long ton.

Stainless steel prices were not expected to improve until markets in Japan and Europe pick up to staunch the flow of material imported into the U.S. - unless domestic stainless mills go ahead and file a dumping suit, a nickel official said.

He noted that the domestic stainless melt in October had edged up. "I am not sure if this was just a glitch or somebody ordered extra material," the official said. The extra volume could also be an attempt by domestic stainless mills to compete more on price against exports, he added.
The slip in LME nickel price will also dampen the scrap market, a stainless scrap merchant said, adding that November to January was traditionally quiet.
Lead shrugged off news that Doe Run's Buick recycling plant has been shut down for about six weeks with the loss of some 6,000 short tons of secondary lead following a roof collapse last week.
"There is extreme pessimism in lead I would associate with a market bottom," a trader said.
Lead premiums were quoted at 3 to 4 cents per pound, unchanged from recent weeks.
